I would like to quote Bjarne Stroustrup here:

I see two primary arguments for using unsigned subscripts and sizes:
• That’s what we have been doing since the adoption of the STL in 1996.
• Sizes cannot be negative
and two primary reasons for using signed subscripts and sizes:
• Signed values are the result of most integer calculations
• In C and C++, unsigned does not model natural numbers

I will dig into the arguments and consider alternatives, but my conclusion stands:
Use signed subscripts and sizes for span as it was deliberately designed to do. The original use of unsigned for the STL was a bad mistake and should be corrected (eventually).

example : 1 - 2 = -1 := by rfl -- passes

This is why formal-conjectures has the answer() elaborator, because it makes 1 - 2 = answer(-1) illegal

Not a solution to the original problem but if the problem is that (2 : Int) is clunky to type, then maybe you could have notation like 2z or 2Z or 2i (admittedly, this last one looks like a complex number) which forces 2 to be an integer. I think Java has stuff like 1000L and 1.3F, and Rust has something similar like 1u32. I can't remember if Lean has something similar.

I recommend 1n, 1z, 1q, 1r, 1c, 1u32, 1u64, 1usize, 1i32, 1i64, and 1isize for (1 : Nat), (1 : Int), (1 : Rat), (1 : Real), (1 : Complex), (1 : UInt32), (1 : USize), (1 : Int32), (1 : Int64), and (1 : ISize) (we should mostly copy rust notation on the fixed size ones). Unsure what the notation should be for Float and Float32. 1i should be invalid notation to avoid looking like an imaginary number. Also 1c for (1 : Complex) might look weird when you mix it with Complex.I

I think this is a significant problem because behavior such as 1 - 2 = 0 and 1 / 0 = 0 is difficult for beginners to anticipate.

Using special notation for subtraction on natural numbers also does not seem very intuitive.

To address this, I wrote a linter that detects subtraction on natural numbers.
GitHub: https://github.com/Seasawher/ValidInputLinter

set_option linter.validInput true

/-- warning: Minus operation on natural numbers detected. -/
#guard_msgs (warning) in
#check 1 - 2

-- Does not trigger the linter because the result type is `Int`.
/-- info: 1 - 2 : Int -/
#guard_msgs in
#check (1 - 2 : Int)

-- This should not trigger the linter warning.
/-- info: 2 - 1 : Nat -/
#guard_msgs in
#check 2 - 1
@Damiano Testa wrote a similar linter which he called papercut

I remember discussing this issue long time ago, and the conclusion was that it is too hard to change (we are not talking just about natural numbers but monoids, subtraction extensions, division fields, ...), and newcomers must adapt, that it is not a real issue because it is my fault that I am lazy to write the types, and if I wrote the types it would be clear...

I would happily support the notation \ (set difference) for natural subtraction, and ÷ for integer division but sadly, I don't see it happening.

I see numerical values just part of the problem. Is it intuitive that 1-2 != 0 but [1].length - [1,2].length = Zero.zero?

Also note that SMT world is way less complicated -- they do not have built-in natural numbers, nor rationals -- everything is either Int, or Real, and it has advantages. Too many different types is often not helping. But I indeed do not see it happening in Lean.

One difference between my linter and the one in leanprover-community/mathlib4#13999 is that mine does not issue a warning for a - b when it can prove that a is greater than or equal to b.

/--
warning: A subtraction `a - b` on `Nat` was detected where `a < b`. Please verify that this is intentional.
-/
#guard_msgs (warning) in
#check 1 - 2

-- does not trigger the linter because the result type is `Int`
#guard_msgs (warning) in
#check (1 - 2 : Int)

-- this should not trigger the linter warning
#guard_msgs (warning) in
#check 2 - 1

/--
warning: A subtraction `a - b` on `Nat` was detected, but it could not be proven that `a ≥ b`.
-/
#guard_msgs (warning) in
#check fun a b : Nat => a - b
